title: Mennonitische Blätter: connecting German Mennonite congregations

date.label: Founded 1 January 1854
date.basis: Christian Neff’s Mennonite Encyclopedia account gives 1 January 1854; the Mennonite Library and Archives serials catalogue independently identifies the Danzig publication as beginning in 1854.

summary: Jakob Mannhardt’s periodical joined historical remembrance, Christian instruction, and news from scattered Mennonite congregations.
paragraphs: Mennonitische Blätter began on 1 January 1854 under Jakob Mannhardt, a Mennonite preacher in Danzig. Its purpose was to help scattered congregations recognize their fellowship and responsibilities toward one another. Mannhardt connected this work with the confession of Christ as the church’s foundation in 1 Corinthians 3:11, the biblical text associated with Menno Simons.

The paper combined accounts of Mennonite history with teaching about faith and congregational order, selections from earlier Anabaptist writings, devotional material, mission reports, hymns, and church news. Remembering the martyrs and attending to the needs of living congregations therefore appeared within the same publication. Its pages became an important record of German Mennonite spiritual and intellectual life.

Mannhardt retired from the editorship in 1874, and Hinrich van der Smissen continued the work for fifty years. Publication was interrupted in 1925 and revived in 1927 under Emil Händiges. The final issue appeared in March 1941 after the German government ordered the paper to stop. The later Hamburg periodical with the same name is a separate serial, distinguished as such in the Mennonite Library and Archives catalogue.

title: P. M. Friesen’s history of the Mennonites in Russia

date.label: German edition published in 1911
date.basis: The Centre for Mennonite Brethren Studies identifies the Raduga edition, Halbstadt, as 1911. The earlier chart transcription reads 1915; the photograph’s small final digit is not used to establish a separate edition.

summary: Peter M. Friesen gathered documents and historical interpretation into a major account of Russian Mennonite church life.
paragraphs: Peter Martin Friesen’s Die Alt-Evangelische Mennonitische Brüderschaft in Russland (1789–1910) was published by Raduga in Halbstadt in 1911. Its title places the Mennonite brotherhood in Russia within the wider history of Mennonites. The Centre for Mennonite Brethren Studies describes twenty-five years of work behind the volume and emphasizes its extensive collection of historical documents.

Friesen wrote as a participant in the life he studied. He had taught at the Halbstadt Zentralschule, served as a Mennonite Brethren minister, and written the church’s 1902 confession of faith. He also sought cooperation between Mennonites and Mennonite Brethren. These commitments help readers understand the standpoint of the historian while distinguishing the documents he preserved from his own interpretation of them.

The surviving archival collection includes part of a handwritten historical manuscript dated 1897 and a 1912 brochure collecting reviews of the published book. An English translation followed in 1978 as The Mennonite Brotherhood in Russia (1789–1910). These identifiable editions establish the publication history. The earlier transcription of the exhibit’s small marker as 1915 is retained as a source-reading discrepancy, rather than used to invent an otherwise unverified 1915 edition.
aliases: Die Alt-Evangelische Mennonitische Brüderschaft in Russland

title: Religiöser Botschafter: an early Mennonite newspaper in America

date.label: Publication began in 1852
date.basis: Mennonite Heritage Center holdings and the Mennonite Library and Archives’ John H. Oberholtzer biography identify the publication and its 1852 beginning.

summary: John H. Oberholtzer’s German-language newspaper opened a durable channel for teaching and communication between American Mennonite congregations.
paragraphs: The partly unreadable Botschafter title on the exhibit can be identified through Mennonite archival sources as Religiöser Botschafter, also styled Der Religiöse Botschafter. John H. Oberholtzer began the paper at Milford Square, Pennsylvania, in 1852. The Mennonite Heritage Center lists surviving issues under this title, while the Mennonite Library and Archives preserves a biography describing Oberholtzer’s labor as writer, editor, typesetter, and printer.

Publishing gave widely separated congregations a way to exchange Christian teaching and discuss common work. Oberholtzer used the press to encourage fellowship, education, and mission. The enterprise continued under the successor title Christliches Volksblatt, linking the early newspaper to the developing network of congregations that formed the General Conference Mennonite Church.

The exhibit calls the 1852 paper the first Mennonite periodical in America. That claim needs a qualification: Heinrich Bertholet had already issued a single number of Der Evangelische Botschafter in 1836. The Mennonite Encyclopedia therefore describes Oberholtzer’s venture as the first successful Mennonite journal. Distinguishing the short-lived 1836 attempt from the sustained 1852 publication preserves both histories without assigning the earlier paper’s title to the later one.

title: Herald of Truth: teaching and news across Mennonite homes

date.basis: Mennonite Church USA Archives preserves the January 1864 first issue’s obituary page; Anabaptist World’s publication history identifies the 1908 sale and merger into Gospel Herald.

summary: John Fretz Funk’s newspaper served the Mennonite Church for forty-four years before joining Gospel Witness to form Gospel Herald.
paragraphs: John Fretz Funk began Herald of Truth in Chicago in January 1864 and moved his publishing work to Elkhart, Indiana, in 1867. An English-language paper and its German companion, Herold der Wahrheit, made printed teaching and news available to Mennonite readers. The Mennonite Church USA Archives preserves material from the first English issue, and the Anabaptist Mennonite Biblical Seminary’s digital collection distinguishes the two language editions.

The paper carried the concerns of Christian households alongside broader church questions. The surviving January 1864 obituary page, for example, joins news of deaths in Ohio and Pennsylvania with funeral Scripture texts and words of Christian hope. Such notices helped readers remember fellow believers beyond their own congregation. During the Civil War, Funk also used the paper to teach nonresistance and examine the responsibilities of Christians facing military demands.

Herald of Truth came to function as an unofficial periodical of the Mennonite Church. Rivalry with Gospel Witness, begun in 1905, coincided with financial difficulties in Funk’s business. In 1908 the new Mennonite Publication Board purchased his periodicals, and Herald of Truth and Gospel Witness were combined as Gospel Herald. The exhibit’s 1864–1908 dates describe the English paper; the German companion has a different publication history and is catalogued separately.

title: The Mennonite Quarterly Review: historical study in service of the church

date.label: First issue under this title: January 1927
date.basis: Goshen College identifies three predecessor supplements in 1926 and the journal’s first volume in 1927; the January 1927 editorial is reproduced in the January 2026 centennial issue.

summary: Harold S. Bender and the Mennonite Historical Society established a lasting forum for Anabaptist and Mennonite historical research.
paragraphs: The Mennonite Quarterly Review began under that title in January 1927 at Goshen College. It grew from the Mennonite Historical Society’s work and Harold S. Bender’s desire to encourage sustained research. Three review supplements to the Goshen College Record had appeared in 1926, so the chart’s 1927 milestone marks the named journal rather than the first appearance of its predecessor.

The opening editorial explained that the journal sought to serve truth and the historic faith and ideals of the Mennonite Church. It did not present itself as a campaign to reshape the church according to an editorial program. Historical inquiry, careful examination of sources, and discussion of books could help believers understand their inheritance and consider their calling in the kingdom of Christ.

The publication developed into a scholarly forum for the Radical Reformation and the histories of Mennonites, Amish, and Hutterites. Its 2026 centennial issue returned to the original editorial and reviewed the journal’s changing questions across successive decades. These later reflections make the early issues readable as the work of particular historians in particular settings, while preserving the documents and arguments for readers to examine.

title: Evangelical Visitor: a printed meeting place for the Brethren in Christ

date.label: First issue: 1 August 1887
date.basis: The Brethren in Christ Archives report in the 2014 General Conference minutes identifies the first issue as 1 August 1887; denominational and historical-society accounts confirm the 1887 beginning.

summary: The Brethren in Christ began Evangelical Visitor to share teaching, news, and the work of congregations separated by distance.
paragraphs: The first Evangelical Visitor appeared on 1 August 1887. General Conference had authorized a church paper, and Henry B. Davidson became its first editor. Working from his home in White Pigeon, Michigan, he sought the cooperation of the publication board and the wider church to supply material and sustain the new undertaking.

The paper offered a common place for Brethren in Christ readers to consider Christian doctrine and practice while keeping in touch with one another. Its pages included denominational news, family announcements, reflections on life in Christ, and accounts of church work. As families and congregations spread across North America and mission work reached farther abroad, these reports helped maintain relationships that could no longer depend on frequent personal visits.

The work also required practical sacrifice. Davidson eventually moved the publishing effort to Abilene, Kansas; the historical-society account preserves his explanation that the move had delayed an issue. He remained editor until 1896. The 1887 marker thus records both an institutional decision to publish and the sustained labor needed to turn that decision into a regular voice within the brotherhood.

title: Der Zionspilger: a Swiss Mennonite paper with readers abroad

date.label: Publication began in 1882
date.basis: The Centre for Mennonite Brethren Studies catalogue and the Swiss Society for Anabaptist History chronology independently give 1882. The photograph’s unreadable year and tentative 1862 transcription do not supply the date.

summary: Der Zionspilger carried the life of Swiss Mennonite congregations into a wider German-reading community, including readers in America.
paragraphs: Der Zionspilger began in 1882, with editorial work at Langnau in the Emmental. The Swiss Society for Anabaptist History places its beginning among developments in the Altevangelische Taufgesinnten congregations, and the Centre for Mennonite Brethren Studies independently catalogues the publication from that year. This evidence supplies the date that cannot be read securely from the photographed timeline.

A contemporary view of its reach appears in H. G. Mannhardt’s 1888 yearbook of Mennonite congregations. The entry for Switzerland describes the Emmental congregation’s paper as appearing twice monthly and lists 2,100 subscribers: 1,700 in Switzerland, 300 in America, and the remaining 100 in France, Germany, and Russia. It also notes that many Swiss subscribers belonged to the state church. The paper’s readership therefore extended beyond both the local congregation and Mennonite membership.

Later issues were published weekly, and the archival catalogue records publication at Evilard after Langnau. Der Zionspilger was succeeded by Perspektive with issue 18, dated 6 May 1990. The contemporary yearbook’s twice-monthly schedule and the later catalogue’s weekly description belong to different stages of the serial’s history; neither requires erasing the other.

title: Maria and Ursula van Beckum: steadfast together in 1544

date.basis: The preserved Martyrs’ Mirror account is headed 1544. Direct enlargement of IMG_9376 also reads 1544, correcting the earlier inventory transcription of 1549. Its Deventer caption is distinguished from the book’s Delden sentencing narrative.

summary: Martyrs’ Mirror remembers Maria and her sister-in-law Ursula refusing to abandon Christ and praying for those who condemned them.
paragraphs: Martyrs’ Mirror relates that Maria van Beckum had taken refuge with her brother John after being driven from home because of her faith. When officers came to arrest her in 1544, she asked her sister-in-law Ursula to accompany her. With John’s consent, Ursula went willingly. The account first brings the women to Deventer, where they answered demands to conform by appealing to the word of God.

The narrative then follows them to Delden. Questioned about baptism, they confessed one baptism according to Christ’s command and the apostles’ practice, joining it to a new life in the Holy Spirit. They described the Lord’s Supper as a remembrance of Christ’s death. The book places their public sentencing at Delden and portrays the women encouraging one another, giving the kiss of peace, and praying that God would forgive their judges.

Maria was burned first. Ursula watched her sister-in-law’s death and refused a further opportunity to renounce her faith. When a block slipped beneath her foot, officials thought she was reconsidering, but she explained the movement and reaffirmed her resolve to hold to Christ. The source presents their companionship, scriptural confession, and prayers for their persecutors as a witness to faithful endurance.

The exhibit’s illustration caption, readable when enlarged, names Ursula van Beckum and gives 1544; an earlier inventory had read the small date as 1549. Its wording locates the burning at Deventer, whereas the preserved book distinguishes Deventer from the later proceedings at Delden. The photograph remains unchanged, and this history keeps that geographical discrepancy visible rather than silently harmonizing the two descriptions.

title: Worship in Pieter Pieters Beckjen’s boat

date.label: c. 1569; sentence dated 26 February 1569
date.basis: The exhibit dates the boat-worship scene approximately to 1569. Martyrs’ Mirror identifies the boatman and preserves his sentence of 26 February 1569; the meetings themselves have no exact date in the account.

summary: An Amsterdam boatman made room for persecuted believers to encourage one another from Scripture, and was condemned for his faith.
paragraphs: The exhibit’s boat-worship scene has a specific counterpart in Martyrs’ Mirror. Pieter Pieters Beckjen, whose name also appears there as Pieter Peters Beckjen, worked as a boatman on the Amstel. Before his execution in 1569, he gathered persecuted believers from around Amsterdam in his boat so that they could strengthen one another in the faith through the word of God.

Van Braght’s account is followed by the text of Beckjen’s death sentence, copied from Amsterdam’s criminal records. It charges him with attending prohibited Mennonite assemblies and twice allowing such meetings in his own boat. It also records his refusal to have his newborn child baptized according to the established church’s ceremonies. Ordinary acts of hospitality, worship, and parental conviction had become grounds for punishment by the authorities.

The sentence is dated 26 February 1569 and orders execution by fire and confiscation of his property. It records that he had been examined and threatened with torture on 17 January. Van Braght remembers his refusal to abandon his confession of Christ and presents the court document so readers can see both that steadfastness and the hostile construction placed upon it by his judges.

The chart describes a ferryman’s boat in Amsterdam harbor and dates the scene approximately to 1569. The book specifies a boatman on the Amstel and gives an exact date for his sentence, but no exact date for the meetings. The approximate scene date is therefore retained without turning the day of his condemnation into a supposed date of worship. Both the narrative and the sentence remain available in their preserved wording.
